findings.text: The first lines tell a newcomer what Athena is, what a study is, and that this page is a sample study. A newcomer can say what they are looking at within three paragraphs.
findings.source: header: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository."

findings.text: The page lives at Athena's URL, but almost everything on it is about firstmate. Athena gets two sentences, and its own value (cost tracking, a second model checking the first) is never shown in action. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena learns mostly about another project.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title> and the lede "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it"

findings.text: The next step is concrete and is also linked from the header. It does not list prerequisites, such as a Rust toolchain or AI model access or keys, so a newcomer cannot tell what setup.sh will need from them.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: Firstmate is explained plainly, and "One piece of work, start to finish" gives a readable walk-through. The same summary appears twice in a row, though: once in this sentence and again, almost word for word, in the first bullet under "What firstmate is".
findings.source: Start here: "Firstmate is a tool that keeps a backlog of programming tasks and hands each one to a separate AI coding tool, called a worker"

findings.text: Some terms arrive before a newcomer can use them. Secondmate is defined only by what it is not, and the page never says what a secondmate is for. Terms like "guarded fast-forward", "exit 75" and "stale wake" also make the middle sections heavy going for a first-time reader.
findings.source: Words used first: "home ... A secondmate is a persistent home of its own, not a task in someone else's backlog."

findings.text: The page openly says where its sources stop, here and in "Limits of this study" ("no failure or retry edge was observed"). This backs up the page's claim that every statement is traceable.
findings.source: Words used first: "in scope ... The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."

findings.text: This note describes how the study was made, not firstmate itself. A newcomer may not know what to make of it, and it may lower their trust in the page without telling them what to do about it.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f3: "A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths"

findings.text: The glossary calls Done "the final state", but the states list has two end states. It also defines captain more narrowly than "Words used first" does. These are small inconsistencies, but a careful reader will notice them.
findings.source: Glossary: "done — The final state" vs States: "Done and Reopened both carry the tag \"ends the task\""
